name: Tawara
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog shows only Borland 1984 subclassification comment; no grammar/phonology of Tawara located.

sources.citation: Chimhundu, Herbert. 2005. 'Doke and the development of Standard Shona', introduction to the ALLEX reprint of Doke 1931a (pp. 8-80 of the PDF text layer).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Second-hand and about standard Shona, not Tawara: says Shona's word marker is 'penultimate length or stress' (after Fortune) and quotes the 1967 orthography commentary that the Shona spoken word carries 'an accent or prominence of extra length (and perhaps extra stress) on the second last syllable' which shifts as affixes are added (PDF text lines ~855-857, 2250-2258).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid tawa1270 and its reference list (13 refs: Doke 1931b; Borland 1984; de Sousa e Silva 1927; dos Santos Júnior 1944, 1945; Ethnologue 2013; Bourdillon 1979a, 1979b, 1982; Ramos de Oliveira 1976; Gelfand 1961, 1962; Dembetembe 1969).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No grammar, sketch or phonology of Tawara itself; the only phonology-typed item is Doke 1931b (Shona-wide).

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2009. Penultimate lengthening in Bantu: analysis and spread. UC Berkeley Phonology Lab Annual Report, 195-209.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Uses standard Shona as the type example of predictable penultimate lengthening (ku-se:k-a, ku-sek-e:s-a..); no mention of Tawara/Tavara or Korekore.

sources.citation: Doke, Clement M. 1931a. Report on the Unification of the Shona Dialects. Hertford: Stephen Austin & Sons (photographic reprint, ALLEX Project / Univ. of Zimbabwe & Univ. of Oslo, 2005, with intro by H. Chimhundu).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Treats Tavara as a member of the Korekore Group (secs. 66-67, pp. 30-31; Northern Tavara in Tete is Nyungwe-influenced, Rhodesian Tavara Korekore-influenced); sec. 122 (p. 62) gives only Tavara consonantal peculiarities; the only stress remark is Shona-wide and generic, sec. 150 (p. 82): 'the function of stress in Bantu is that of word-building. In each word or word-group in Bantu there is one, and only one, main stress' — no statement of where it falls; Appendix IV vocabularies (incl. two Tavara lists) mark tone, not stress or length.
